title: The crown (Mark 15:1–20)
hookLine: Barabbas released, the purple cloak, the crown of thorns

cards: Early in the morning, the chief priests, the elders and the scribes hold a council, bind Jesus, and hand him over to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. The sentence will be his to give.
Pilate has a custom at the feast: he releases one prisoner, whoever the crowd asks for. In his jail is Barabbas, locked up with rebels who committed murder in an uprising.
Pilate offers the crowd a choice: Jesus, or Barabbas? And before long, soldiers will put a crown on Jesus's head. Not gold.

teach.h: ART THOU THE KING? THOU SAYEST IT.
teach.b: First, Pilate's question, in the Douay-Rheims: "Art thou the king of the Jews?" Jesus answers: "Thou sayest it." Then he's silent again while the chief priests accuse him of many things, and Pilate marvels.
Second, the choice. Pilate seems to see that the charge comes out of envy. But the chief priests stir up the crowd to ask for Barabbas.
What shall I do with this king, then? Crucify him.
Wanting to satisfy the crowd, Pilate releases Barabbas, has Jesus scourged, and hands him over to be crucified.
Some readers hear something in the prisoner's name: bar abba, Aramaic for son of the father, and last night Jesus called God Abba.
If that's right, one son of the father walks free this morning, and the other takes his place. Third, the crown. Roman soldiers lead him into the governor's palace and call together the whole cohort.
"And they clothe him with purple, and platting a crown of thorns, they put it upon him. And they began to salute him: Hail, king of the Jews." Purple is a king's color; that's the joke.
They hit his head with a reed, spit on him, and kneel in mock worship. Fourth, the irony.

teach.h: AND PLATTING A CROWN OF THORNS.
teach.b: They mean every piece as a joke: the purple cloak, the crown, the salute, the kneeling. In Mark's telling, every piece is true: he really is the king, and the soldiers are acting out a coronation without knowing it.
Catholics remember this scene in the rosary, the third Sorrowful Mystery, the crowning with thorns. It was Rome's soldiers who mocked him, and Rome that crucified him.

how: Catholics meditate on the crowning with thorns as the third Sorrowful Mystery of the rosary, and visiting the imprisoned is one of the Church's corporal works of mercy, carried out through prison ministries in many dioceses.

games.q: you're Pilate. the crowd shouts for Barabbas, a rebel. you suspect the charge against Jesus is envy. what do you do?
o: release Barabbas to satisfy the crowd.
games.why: wanting to satisfy the crowd, Pilate releases Barabbas, has Jesus scourged, and hands him over to be crucified.

practice: Jesus was a prisoner that morning: bound, mocked, beaten, with no one to speak for him.
People sit in prison cells right now, some guilty, some not, some forgotten by everyone; bring one to mind, or picture a cell and someone in it this morning.
If you pray, you can pray for them and for the people who guard them; if you don't, simply hold them in mind for a minute.

wordCard.voice: The crown. The crown of thorns Roman soldiers pressed on Jesus's head, hailing him as king. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a crown of thorns. stephanos, crown, gives us the name Stephen.

carryVoice: Your line: they mocked the king. Thorns for a crown. Until tomorrow.
